subtopics.title: Force, transmissibility and moment
subtopics.theory_md:
A **force** is a vector, fixed by four things: **magnitude, direction, sense** (push or pull) and **point of application**.

**Principle of transmissibility:** on a rigid body, a force may be moved to any point **along its line of action** without changing its external effect (equilibrium or motion). Internal stresses do change, and moving it off the line is not allowed.

**Moment** of a force about a point: $M = F\times d$, with $d$ the perpendicular distance from the point to the line of action. Unit N$\cdot$m; it measures the turning effect, clockwise or anticlockwise. A force through the point has zero moment. For a force at $(x,y)$: $M_O = xF_y - yF_x$.
subtopics.basics_md: A spanner turns a nut better when you hold it at the far end: the same push, a longer perpendicular distance, a bigger turning effect. That turning effect is the moment.
key_points: Force is characterised by magnitude, direction, sense and point of application
Transmissibility: a force can slide along its line of action on a rigid body, external effect unchanged
Moment = force x perpendicular distance, unit N.m, with a sense (clockwise or anticlockwise)
Moment measures the turning effect; a force through the point has zero moment

subtopics.title: Varignon's theorem (law of moments)
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** the algebraic sum of the moments of coplanar forces about any point equals the moment of their resultant about that point: $\sum M_O = R\,d$.

**Proof (two forces $P$, $Q$ meeting at A; any point O, $AO=d$):** take the x-axis along AO. Only y-components have a moment, with arm $d$:
$M_P = d\,P\sin\theta_1,\ M_Q = d\,Q\sin\theta_2,\ M_R = d\,R\sin\theta$.
Resolving, $R\sin\theta = P\sin\theta_1 + Q\sin\theta_2$. Multiply by $d$: $M_R = M_P + M_Q$. For more forces, combine two at a time.

**Use:** the line of action of a resultant is at $d = \sum M_O/R$; for equilibrium $\sum M=0$ about any point.
subtopics.basics_md: Pushing a door with two hands at different spots gives the same turning as one equal push at the right spot. Varignon says exactly that: add the turning effects of the parts and you get the turning effect of the whole.
key_points: Statement: sum of moments of forces about a point = moment of the resultant about that point
Proof: x-axis along AO, only y-components give moment, R sin(theta) = P sin(theta1) + Q sin(theta2), multiply by d
Extends to any number of forces by combining two at a time
Use: position of the resultant, d = sum M / R

subtopics.title: Couple and its properties
subtopics.theory_md:
A **couple** is a pair of **equal, opposite, parallel, non-collinear** forces. Its resultant force is zero, so it produces pure rotation.

**Couple moment:** $M = F\times d$, $d$ = perpendicular distance between the forces (the arm), N$\cdot$m.

**Properties:**
1. Resultant force is zero; it cannot be replaced by a single force, only balanced by an equal and opposite couple.
2. Its moment is the **same about every point** of the plane (a free vector).
3. It may be moved anywhere in its plane, or to a parallel plane, without changing its effect.
4. Two couples of equal moment are equivalent.

**Proof of 2:** about a point at distance $x$ outside the pair: $F(x+d) - Fx = Fd$; between the forces: $Fx + F(d-x) = Fd$.
subtopics.basics_md: Turning a steering wheel with both hands pushes one side up and one down by equal amounts. Nothing moves sideways; the wheel only rotates. That pair is a couple.
key_points: Couple = two equal, opposite, parallel, non-collinear forces; resultant force zero
Moment M = F x d, same about every point in the plane
Only another couple can balance a couple
Can be shifted anywhere in its plane without changing its effect

subtopics.title: Forces as vectors: addition and components
subtopics.theory_md:
A force is a **vector**: it has magnitude, direction and sense, and adds by the **parallelogram law** (or triangle law). Mass and time are scalars.

**Characteristics of a force:** magnitude, direction, sense, point of application.

**Parallelogram law:** two forces $P$, $Q$ at angle $\theta$ have the resultant along the diagonal:
$R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$, $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$ ($\alpha$ from $P$).

**Components:** $F_x = F\cos\theta$, $F_y = F\sin\theta$. In 3D, $F_x = F\,\ell_x/L$ with $\ell_x$ the x-extent and $L$ the length of the line of action.
subtopics.basics_md: Walking 3 m east then 4 m north puts you 5 m from the start, not 7 m. Directions matter when you add vectors.

subtopics.title: Dot product, cross product and moment as r x F
subtopics.theory_md:
**Unit vector** along $\vec A$: $\hat a = \vec A/|\vec A|$.

**Dot product** (scalar): $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$. Zero for perpendicular vectors; gives the angle and the component of one vector along another.

**Cross product** (vector): $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta$, direction by the right-hand rule, $\vec A\times\vec B = -\vec B\times\vec A$; evaluated as the determinant of $(\hat i,\hat j,\hat k)$, $A$, $B$.

**Moment of a force about O:** $\vec M_O = \vec r\times\vec F$, $\vec r$ from O to any point on the line of action. Its magnitude is $F\,d$.
subtopics.basics_md: Dot product asks how much two arrows point the same way and gives a number. Cross product asks how much they sweep across each other and gives a new arrow at right angles, which is why a moment points along the axis of rotation.

Cross product is a vector of magnitude AB sin(theta), direction by right-hand rule; A x B = -B x A
Moment of a force about O is M = r x F with r from O to the line of action
Use the determinant of i, j, k to evaluate the cross product

subtopics.title: Resultant of a coplanar force system
subtopics.theory_md:
Coplanar systems are **concurrent** (lines meet at a point), **parallel**, or **general non-concurrent**.

Steps for the resultant:
1. Resolve: $\Sigma F_x$, $\Sigma F_y$.
2. $R = \sqrt{(\Sigma F_x)^2 + (\Sigma F_y)^2}$, $\tan\theta = |\Sigma F_y/\Sigma F_x|$; the signs give the quadrant.
3. Moments about a point O: $\Sigma M_O$. By Varignon, $R\,d = \Sigma M_O$, so $d = \Sigma M_O/R$.
4. Where it cuts an axis: on the x-axis $x = \Sigma M_O/\Sigma F_y$; on the y-axis $y = \Sigma M_O/\Sigma F_x$.

A force through O has no moment about O; a force along an axis has no moment about a point on it. Pick O to kill as many terms as possible.

subtopics.title: Types of loading and equivalent point loads
subtopics.theory_md:
**Loads on a beam:** concentrated (point) load, **UDL** (constant intensity $w$ kN/m), **UVL** (intensity varying linearly; triangular if zero at one end) and applied couples.

Replace a distributed load by one force equal to the **area of the load diagram**, acting through its **centroid**:
- UDL over $L$: $wL$ at $L/2$.
- Triangular load (zero to $w$): $\tfrac12 wL$ at $L/3$ from the larger end ($2L/3$ from the zero end).
- Trapezoid ($w_1$ to $w_2$): split into a rectangle $w_1L$ and a triangle $\tfrac12(w_2-w_1)L$.

Use the equivalent loads in $\Sigma M$ and $\Sigma F$.

subtopics.title: Dam stability and the middle-third rule
subtopics.theory_md:
A dam is acted on by the **water thrust** (horizontal, $\Sigma H$), its **weight** and other vertical loads ($\Sigma V$, uplift counted upward), all about the heel O.

1. $R=\sqrt{(\Sigma H)^2+(\Sigma V)^2}$, $\tan\theta = \Sigma V/\Sigma H$.
2. $\Sigma M_O$ of all forces (same sense for thrust and weight about the heel).
3. The resultant cuts the base at $\bar x = \Sigma M_O/\Sigma V$ from O.

**Middle-third rule:** the dam is safe (no tension in the base) if $\bar x$ lies between $B/3$ and $2B/3$ from the heel, i.e. eccentricity $e\le B/6$. If the resultant falls outside the middle third, tension appears at one edge of the base.

subtopics.title: Parallelogram, triangle and polygon laws
subtopics.theory_md:
**Parallelogram law:** if two forces at a point are the adjacent sides of a parallelogram (in magnitude and direction), their resultant is the diagonal through that point.

$R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2+2PQ\cos\theta}$, $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P+Q\cos\theta}$ ($\alpha$ measured from $P$).

**Proof:** in parallelogram OACB, drop CD perpendicular to OA produced: $AD=Q\cos\theta$, $CD=Q\sin\theta$; $OC^2=(P+Q\cos\theta)^2+(Q\sin\theta)^2$.

Special cases: $\theta=0$: $R=P+Q$; $\theta=90^\circ$: $R=\sqrt{P^2+Q^2}$; $\theta=180^\circ$: $R=|P-Q|$; $P=Q$: $R=2P\cos(\theta/2)$, along the bisector.

**Triangle law:** two forces as two sides in order; the closing side is the resultant. **Polygon law:** same for many forces.

subtopics.title: Resolution versus composition; resolved part of a resultant
subtopics.theory_md:
**Composition:** many forces into **one resultant** (unique): parallelogram, triangle, polygon laws, or analytically.
**Resolution:** one force into **components** (not unique; usually two perpendicular): $F_x=F\cos\theta$, $F_y=F\sin\theta$. They are inverse operations.

Along a line making angle $\varphi$ with a force, the component is $F\cos\varphi$ and the perpendicular component $F\sin\varphi$.

**Resolved-parts theorem:** the sum of the resolved parts of forces in any direction equals the resolved part of their resultant in that direction:
$R\cos(\alpha-\varphi)=\Sigma F_i\cos(\theta_i-\varphi)$.

Along two **non-perpendicular** directions, use the sine rule (Lami) on the triangle of forces.
subtopics.basics_md: A pull on a rope tied to a sled's front can be thought of as part pulling forward and part lifting upward. Splitting a push into parts like this is resolution; putting parts back into one push is composition.

Components are not unique; usually taken along perpendicular axes

Resolved part of the resultant = algebraic sum of resolved parts of the forces

subtopics.title: The free body diagram
subtopics.theory_md:
A **free body diagram (FBD)** is a sketch of a body (or part of a structure) **isolated** from its surroundings, with **every external force** on it shown: applied loads, self-weight (at the centre of gravity) and the **reactions** that replace supports and contacts.

Steps: isolate the body; draw the weight; replace each support or contact by its reaction; mark dimensions and angles; then write $\Sigma F_x=0$, $\Sigma F_y=0$, $\Sigma M=0$.

Reaction directions: smooth surface, normal to the surface; string, tension along the string away from the body; hinge, $H$ and $V$; fixed end, $H$, $V$ and $M$; friction along the surface.

Ladder against a smooth wall on rough floor ($\theta$ with floor, length $L$, weight $W$): $R_f=W$, $F=R_w$, $R_w=\tfrac{W}{2}\cot\theta$.

subtopics.theory_md:
For smooth spheres or cylinders the reaction at a contact is **normal to the surfaces**: through the centre for a wall or floor contact, along the **line of centres** between two bodies.

Method:
1. Geometry: horizontal gap between centres $=b-r_1-r_2$ (in a channel), centre distance $=r_1+r_2$, so $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{gap}}{r_1+r_2}$ with $\theta$ the angle of the line of centres with the horizontal.

3. FBD of the lower body: add $R$ (reversed) to its weight and the other reactions; use $\Sigma F_x=0$, $\Sigma F_y=0$.

subtopics.title: Replacing a force by a force and a couple
subtopics.theory_md:
A force $F$ can be moved **parallel to itself** to another point B if a **couple** is added whose moment equals the moment of the original force about B: $M = F\times d$, $d$ the perpendicular distance from B to the line of action.

Procedure: put the same force $F$ at B (same magnitude, direction, sense) and add the couple $M_B$ with the **same sense** as the moment of $F$ about B.

The new force at B and the couple together are equivalent to the original force. This is the reverse of finding a single resultant, and it is how loads are carried to a support (the 500 N load at a bracket becomes a force plus a moment at the wall).
subtopics.basics_md: Pushing a door at its edge is the same as pushing the hinge with that force plus twisting the hinge. Moving a force sideways always costs a twist equal to force times the shift.

- $R=0$, $M_O\neq0$: a **pure couple**, the same about every point.
- $R=0$, $M_O=0$: **equilibrium**.

Moment of a force at $(x,y)$: $M_O=xF_y-yF_x$.

subtopics.title: Condition for the resultant to pass through a point
subtopics.theory_md:
The resultant of a system passes through a point D **if and only if** the total moment about D is zero: $\Sigma M_D=0$.

To make a given system's resultant pass through D with an unknown force $P$ applied at A:
1. Write $\Sigma M_D=0$ with $P$'s moment as $P\,d_P$.
2. For a given moment, $P$ is **least when its arm $d_P$ is greatest**. The greatest arm about D is the distance AD, reached when $P$ is **perpendicular to AD**.
3. $P_{min}=\dfrac{\text{moment of the other forces about D}}{AD}$.
subtopics.basics_md: If a push passes through a pivot it cannot turn it. To make the combined push go through D, the other pushes' turning about D must be cancelled; the cheapest way is to push as far from D as possible, at a right angle to the line to D.

subtopics.title: Conditions of equilibrium and support reactions
subtopics.theory_md:
A rigid body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and resultant moment are both zero.

**2D:** $\Sigma F_x=0$, $\Sigma F_y=0$, $\Sigma M=0$ (3 equations). Concurrent forces need only two; parallel forces need two ($\Sigma F$ and $\Sigma M$).
**3D:** $\Sigma F_x=\Sigma F_y=\Sigma F_z=0$ and $\Sigma M_x=\Sigma M_y=\Sigma M_z=0$ (6 equations).

**Support reaction:** the force (and moment at a fixed support) a support develops to keep the structure in equilibrium.

**Determinate:** unknown reactions $\le$ number of equations (simply supported, cantilever, overhanging beam). **Indeterminate:** more unknowns (fixed beam, propped cantilever, continuous beam); extra deflection conditions are needed.

A **two-force member** carries a force along the line joining its two points.
subtopics.basics_md: A body that is not moving needs two things: no net push (so it does not slide) and no net twist (so it does not spin). Count the unknowns against the equations: if they match, statics alone is enough.

subtopics.title: Lami's theorem and three-force equilibrium
subtopics.theory_md:
**Lami's theorem:** if three **coplanar, concurrent** forces keep a body in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the **sine of the angle between the other two**:
$\dfrac{P}{\sin\alpha}=\dfrac{Q}{\sin\beta}=\dfrac{R}{\sin\gamma}$, with $\alpha$ between $Q,R$; $\beta$ between $R,P$; $\gamma$ between $P,Q$ ($\alpha+\beta+\gamma=360^\circ$).

**Proof:** the forces form a closed triangle (sides parallel to $P,Q,R$); its interior angles are $180^\circ-\alpha$, $180^\circ-\beta$, $180^\circ-\gamma$. The sine rule and $\sin(180^\circ-\theta)=\sin\theta$ give the result.

Use for **exactly three** forces. For a smooth contact the reaction is normal; for a string the tension is along the string. For more forces, resolve instead.
subtopics.basics_md: Three pulls on a knot that stays still must close up into a triangle. In that triangle the sine rule links each side to the opposite angle, and that is Lami's theorem.

subtopics.title: Support reactions of beams
subtopics.theory_md:
Method for a beam:
1. **FBD:** replace the supports by reactions (hinge $H_A$, $V_A$; roller $R_B$ **normal to its surface**, so along the vertical for a horizontal surface and at the incline's normal otherwise).
2. Replace UDLs and UVLs by point loads at their centroids; resolve inclined loads; a couple enters $\Sigma M$ as itself.
3. $\Sigma M_A=0$ (the hinge, to eliminate $H_A$ and $V_A$) gives the roller force.
4. $\Sigma F_y=0$ gives $V_A$; $\Sigma F_x=0$ gives $H_A$.
5. Check with $\Sigma M_B=0$.

Vertical loads on a vertical-roller beam give $H_A=0$. A roller on a slope $\tan\alpha$ contributes a **horizontal thrust** $R_B\sin\alpha$.

subtopics.title: Rods, levers, wedges and rolling bodies
subtopics.theory_md:
These are all solved by an FBD and the three equations, choosing the moment point to remove unknowns.

- **Rod or lever on a hinge:** moments about the hinge give the string/force; the hinge reaction follows from $\Sigma F$.
- **Two-force member** (a link pinned at both ends, no load between): its force is along the line of the pins.
- **Roller turning over a step:** at the moment of turning, the ground reaction is zero; take moments about the step corner C. The force is least when perpendicular to OC (arm $=r$).
- **Wedge with friction:** each contact has normal reaction plus friction, a single resultant at the friction angle $\phi$ from the normal, opposing slip.
- **Bar on smooth wall and incline:** the reactions are normal; moments about one end give the angle.
